reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight centers on how sensory data—specifically double images—are not inherently perceived but emerge from a dynamic interplay between raw neural input and learned interpretation. Initially, the brain processes disparate retinal signals as unified wholes, reflecting a fundamental confusion kernel. Over time, this confusion dissolves through cognitive training, aligning with Bayesian principles where prior beliefs modulate new sensory evidence. The anti-sensationalist stance challenges whether such phenomena qualify as true sensations, yet the counterargument posits that even seemingly simple perceptions require active discrimination—an operation akin to signal processing in information theory. This duality implies that perception is not passive reception but an active inference process shaped by both bottom-up sensory fidelity and top-down conceptual frameworks. The failure mode occurs when knowledge fails to override initial sensory ambiguity, leading to perceptual instability or hallucination-like states.
